title: How Can Physiotherapy Support Recovery After a C-Section?
description: Early caesarean mobility tips and later graded rehab—wound care stays with your surgical team; physiotherapy helps movement once healing allows.
primaryQuestion: How can physiotherapy support recovery after a caesarean?
directAnswer: After a caesarean you are recovering from major abdominal surgery while caring for a newborn, so wound and activity limits from your surgical and maternity team come first. UK NHS recovery advice encourages getting up and moving as soon as possible, a daily walk to lower clot risk, and only restarting driving, exercise, heavy carrying or sex when you feel able—which may not be for about six weeks. Physiotherapy later helps with bed transfers, coughing support, pelvic-floor and abdominal loading, and graded return to activity once medical healing allows—it does not replace obstetric review for infection, bleeding or wound problems.

sections.heading: Early mobility and daily tasks
paragraphs: While you are still in hospital, NHS guidance says you are encouraged to get out of bed and move around as soon as possible, with pain relief to make breathing and short walks manageable. At home, try to stay mobile with gentle daily walking without overexerting. Supporting the wound with a folded towel or your hands when you cough or laugh can make those moments less frightening.

Getting from lying to sitting by rolling onto your side and pushing up with your arms usually feels kinder than a straight sit-up. Practise once with a nurse before discharge if you can. Clarify stair advice for your home, who can carry the baby on stairs at first, and your team’s lifting limits—NHS notes you should be able to hold and carry your baby, but may not manage loads heavier than the baby straight away.

Wound care follows your midwife’s instructions: gently clean and dry the wound, wear loose comfortable clothes, and watch for infection signs. Do not begin scar massage, oils or vigorous abdominal drills over an open, leaking or unexplained painful wound. Timing of any later scar work belongs with a clinician after the wound has closed—there is no universal massage calendar to invent here.

sections.heading: Later graded rehabilitation
paragraphs: Once you feel able and your maternity team agrees, progress walking distance gradually and notice how you feel the next day. Pelvic-floor exercises can begin when comfortable. Gentle abdominal awareness and everyday strength—sit-to-stand, carrying the baby, posture for feeding—come before high-impact classes. Our guide on when to exercise after delivery covers impact readiness across birth types; this guide covers movement support specific to a caesarean birth.

UK NHS wording is clear that restarting exercise and similar activities happens when you feel able and they are not uncomfortable, which may not be for six weeks or so—not a hard deadline for everyone, and not a race. Complications, anaemia or a difficult labour can lengthen the ramp. Stop any drill that sharply pulls the wound, increases bleeding, causes dizziness or creates pelvic heaviness.

Dr. Zalak Shah (PT) can review breathing, abdominal-wall behaviour under light load, pelvic-floor function and readiness for graded strengthening after medical clearance where it applies. Surgical complications and wound infection stay with your maternity surgeons; at Women’s Health Duo that medical lane is Dr. Charmi Shah when obstetric input is needed.

sections.heading: Wound, infection and clot warning signs
paragraphs: Contact your midwife or GP straight away for severe pain, leaking urine, pain when peeing, heavy vaginal bleeding, a wound that becomes more red, painful and swollen, pus or foul discharge from the wound, a cough or shortness of breath, or swelling or pain in a lower leg. NHS recovery pages list these as possible infection or blood-clot signs that need prompt treatment.

Collapse, uncontrolled haemorrhage, severe chest pain or sudden difficulty breathing are emergencies—use local emergency services rather than waiting for a routine message reply. After acute problems are treated, graded movement advice can resume.

faqs.question: When can I exercise after a caesarean?
faqs.answer: NHS advice is to start gentle mobility early as encouraged by your team, and to return to formal exercise only when you feel able and it is comfortable—which may not be for about six weeks. Your surgeon’s instructions and any complications always outrank a generic online timeline.

faqs.question: Should I massage my caesarean scar early on?
faqs.answer: Not while the wound is open, leaking or medically concerning. Follow wound-care advice first. Scar mobilisation, when appropriate, waits until a clinician confirms the wound has healed enough—there is no single day that fits everyone.
